title: Make event delivery understandable
question: How can people tell whether an event is waiting, retrying, or finished?
summary: Keep the existing queue and worker. Add an explicit delivery lifecycle and a small status view so people can distinguish a delayed event from a failed one. Agree on retry ownership before building the view.
scope: Synthetic research example only. No customer payloads, real incidents, cloud accounts, or live source systems were queried. Current means current within this fixture; the proposed behavior has not been implemented or tested.

sections.title: The domain before the infrastructure
paragraphs: An event describes something that happened. A delivery is the attempt to notify a destination about that event. One event can have several deliveries, and one delivery can have several attempts.

Think of the event as a letter and the delivery as the tracked shipment. Retrying the shipment should not create a new letter. Event identity must survive retries so the destination can recognize duplicates.
details: Entities: Event, Delivery and Attempt. The producer owns event creation; the worker owns an attempt; the destination owns acceptance. The delivery lifecycle is waiting -> attempting -> succeeded, with retrying or failed outcomes when an attempt cannot complete.
The queue provides transport. It does not own the business definition of success. A message disappearing from a queue is not enough evidence that the destination accepted it.

sections.title: What happens today
paragraphs: The producer sends an event to the queue. A worker reads it and calls the destination. In this fixture, people can see that a delivery is pending, but cannot tell whether a callback is running or waiting for a retry.

Synthetic example: event evt_demo_001 asks a destination to refresh a demonstration record. The destination times out. The record stays pending, so a person has to inspect logs to learn what happened.
details: The fixture establishes the visible pending state and the timeout path. It does not establish deployed retry intervals, actual traffic volume, or production failure rates.
A log query without the event correlation ID can miss the relevant attempt. Empty log results should be reported as incomplete evidence, not as proof the worker never ran.

sections.title: The smallest useful change
paragraphs: Record each delivery attempt and expose its state. The view should answer: what happened, when did the last attempt run, and is another attempt expected? Keep payloads out of the status view.

The queue and worker remain the transport path. Persisted delivery state becomes the explanation path. A timeout can be shown as retrying only when retry policy actually schedules another attempt; otherwise it is failed.
details: This is a proposal with medium confidence (~70%). It fits the synthetic evidence, but ownership, retention, expected volume and destination idempotency still need a decision.
No cloud vendor or new service is selected. Reuse the project's existing storage when it can represent this lifecycle cheaply. Add infrastructure only when workload evidence requires it.

sections.title: Failure paths and ownership
paragraphs: A duplicate event must keep the same identity. A late response must not turn a succeeded delivery back into a failed one. Permission checks must prevent one organization from seeing another organization's delivery history.
After migration, old pending records may lack attempt evidence. Label them as legacy or unknown until verified. Do not infer success from their age or from an empty queue.
details: Observe producer -> queue -> worker -> destination using correlation IDs and timestamps. Mark where observation ends. The status record should contain metadata needed for explanation, not raw customer request/response bodies.
A rollback can disable the new view while preserving collected attempt metadata. Decide retention and reconciliation rules before migrating existing records.

options.name: Keep pending + logs
options.tradeoff: People still need an engineer to explain delays
options.confidence: High within this fixture; no production frequency data

options.name: Delivery lifecycle + view
options.benefit: Explains outcomes while reusing the transport path
options.tradeoff: Needs ownership, retention and reconciliation rules

options.name: Replace the event platform
options.benefit: Could add orchestration for broader requirements
options.tradeoff: Adds migration and operating cost without workload evidence
options.confidence: Low; scope and cost are not established

plan.title: Settle lifecycle ownership
plan.outcome: The team agrees what each state means and who can change it
plan.dependsOn: Producer and worker ownership; retry policy
plan.check: A timeout, duplicate and late success each have an agreed state transition

plan.title: Capture attempt metadata
plan.outcome: An event can be traced without exposing payloads
plan.dependsOn: Lifecycle decision and existing storage constraints
plan.check: Synthetic success/failure/retry attempts retain one event ID and distinct attempt IDs

plan.title: Build the authorized status view
plan.outcome: A person sees the last outcome and next expected action
plan.check: A synthetic failure is understandable; a different tenant cannot read it

plan.title: Roll out and reconcile legacy records
plan.outcome: New records are explained and old unknowns remain visible
plan.check: Legacy records stay explicitly unknown; disabling the view preserves recorded evidence

questions: Who owns the retry schedule and the terminal failure decision?
How long should metadata be kept, and what workload is expected?
Does the destination already enforce event idempotency?
